title: Polymer Genome in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is redefining the landscape of polymer science. Although numerous AI applications have been introduced in this field, the roles of polymer encoding strategies and different applications of AI models in polymer design remain insufficiently understood. Here, we build upon the foundation of polymer databases to critically examine the performance and applicability of current encoding strategies across different use cases. We then focus on two major AI application domains, property prediction and inverse design, to evaluate the strengths, weaknesses and suitable scenarios for various model architectures. Finally, we emphasize the significance of the online platforms for promoting data accessibility and accelerating the migration from experience-based discovery toward AI-driven innovation in polymer science and engineering. Through these discussions, we aim to provide practical guidance for future research and development in AI-assisted polymer design.
summary: This paper reviews the state-of-the-art in using Artificial Intelligence to advance polymer science, focusing heavily on the crucial role of molecular encoding strategies. It compares fingerprint, graph, and sequence-based representations for tasks like property prediction and inverse design. The work stresses that standardized, comprehensive databases and better encoding are necessary to move polymer discovery from empirical to AI-driven innovation.
main_problem: The field of AI-driven polymer science is lagging due to the structural complexity of polymers, requiring better encoding strategies for AI models.
main_result: The paper provides a critical review and practical guidance on leveraging advanced AI techniques for polymer design, emphasizing the need for standardized, multi-scale data.
method: The authors critically examine various AI encoding strategies (Fingerprint, Graph, Sequence) and model architectures (GNNs, Transformers, LLMs) applied to polymer property prediction and inverse design.
model_or_system: The physical system is polymers (homopolymers, copolymers, blends). The models involve deep learning architectures like Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Transformers, operating on molecular representations.
key_observables: Polymer properties such as glass transition temperature ($T_g$), mechanical strength, and electronic/dielectric properties.
important_parameters: Polymerization degree, structural connectivity (2D/3D graphs), and chemical composition.
main_assumptions: The choice of encoding must align with data availability and the structural complexity of the polymer system.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares polymer databases based on data coverage and property inclusion; Table 1 summarizes common encoding strategies (Fingerprint, Graph, Sequence) for various tasks.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first identifying the gap in AI application to polymers, then detailing the evolution and comparison of encoding strategies, evaluating model applicability in property prediction and inverse design, and concluding with recommendations for data infrastructure.
why_interesting: While focused on polymers, the core methodology—applying advanced ML/AI (GNNs, Transformers, LLMs) to complex, high-dimensional structural data—is highly relevant to modeling quantum many-body systems or disordered quantum materials.

Figure 4. Representative generative models for polymer design. (a) Variational Autoencoder (VAE). Encodes polymers into a continuous latent space, where new structures are generated by sampling latent vectors and decoding them into valid representations. (b) Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM). Consists of a forward diffusion process (curved arrow) adding noise and a reverse denoising process (straight arrow) that gradually reconstructs polymer structures from Gaussian noise. (c) Transformer-based model. Learns polymer sequence representations and generates polymers through autoregressive decoding.
